q: In its first year of operations, Arch Co. recorded book depreciation of $100,000 and tax depreciation of $160,000 on its equipment. There are no other differences, and the enacted tax rate for all years is 25%. What amount of deferred income tax expense should Arch report?
exp: The $60,000 excess of tax over book depreciation is a taxable temporary difference that creates a deferred tax liability of $60,000 x 25% = $15,000. $40,000 and $25,000 apply the rate to each depreciation amount separately rather than to the difference.

q: Bale Corp. reported pretax financial income of $800,000, which included $40,000 of municipal bond interest. Tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation by $60,000. The enacted tax rate is 25% for all years. What total income tax expense should Bale report?
exp: Total expense = (pretax income - permanent differences) x rate = ($800,000 - $40,000) x 25% = $190,000, made up of current tax $175,000 ($700,000 x 25%) and deferred tax $15,000. $175,000 is only the current portion.

q: At December 31, Year 1, Cole Co. had a $300,000 taxable temporary difference that will reverse equally in Years 2, 3, and 4. Enacted tax rates are 25% for Years 2 and 3 and 21% for Year 4; a bill proposing 19% for Year 4 has not been enacted. What deferred tax liability should Cole report at December 31, Year 1?
exp: Deferred taxes are measured using enacted rates for the years in which the differences reverse (ASC 740-10-30-8): $100,000 x 25% + $100,000 x 25% + $100,000 x 21% = $71,000. Proposed but unenacted rates are ignored, so $69,000 (using 19%) is wrong.

q: At year-end, Dyer Co. had gross deferred tax assets of $200,000. Based on the weight of available evidence, it is more likely than not that $60,000 of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. What net deferred tax asset should Dyer report?
exp: A valuation allowance is recorded for the portion of deferred tax assets that is more likely than not (over 50%) to go unrealized: $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000 (ASC 740-10-30-5). Writing off the whole asset applies a stricter threshold than the standard requires.

q: Under current U.S. GAAP, how should a company classify its deferred tax liabilities and assets on a classified balance sheet?
choices: Current or noncurrent based on the classification of the related asset or liability
Current or noncurrent based on the expected reversal date
All as noncurrent
All as current
exp: ASU 2015-17 requires all deferred tax assets and liabilities to be classified as noncurrent, netted by jurisdiction. Classifying by the related asset or liability was the superseded rule.

q: Which of the following creates a deferred tax asset?
choices: Using an installment sale method for tax for a sale recognized in full for book
Taking accelerated depreciation for tax and straight-line for book
Deducting a prepaid expense for tax when paid while expensing it for book over the coverage period
Receiving rent in advance that is taxable when received but recognized for book when earned
exp: Advance rent is taxed now but will be book income later, so future taxable income will be smaller; that future deductible amount is a deferred tax asset. The other three items defer taxable income or accelerate deductions, which creates deferred tax liabilities.

q: In Year 1, Eads Co. accrued $50,000 of warranty expense for book purposes and paid $20,000 of warranty claims, which are deductible for tax only when paid. The enacted tax rate is 25% for all years. By how much should Eads's deferred tax asset increase in Year 1?
exp: The unpaid accrual of $30,000 ($50,000 - $20,000) is a deductible temporary difference: $30,000 x 25% = $7,500. $12,500 applies the rate to the full accrual, but $20,000 has already been deducted on the tax return.

q: Which of the following is a permanent difference rather than a temporary difference?
choices: Warranty costs accrued for book purposes but deducted for tax when paid
Premiums on officers' life insurance for which the corporation is the beneficiary
Depreciation computed using MACRS for tax and straight-line for book
Subscription revenue received in advance and taxed when received
exp: Life insurance premiums where the company is the beneficiary are never deductible, and the proceeds are never taxable, so the difference never reverses and creates no deferred tax. The other items reverse over time and are temporary differences.

q: In Year 1, Fane Co., a calendar-year C corporation, incurred a net operating loss of $400,000 for federal tax purposes. The enacted federal rate is 21%, and it is more likely than not that the full loss will be used against future taxable income. How should Fane account for the NOL in Year 1?
choices: Recognize a refund receivable of $84,000 from carrying the loss back two years
Recognize no benefit until the loss is used
Recognize a deferred tax asset of $67,200, because carryforwards are limited to 80% of taxable income
Recognize a deferred tax asset and an income tax benefit of $84,000
exp: Federal NOLs arising after 2020 generally cannot be carried back but may be carried forward indefinitely, so the carryforward creates a deferred tax asset of $400,000 x 21% = $84,000, less any needed valuation allowance (ASC 740-10-25). The 80% of taxable income limit affects when the NOL is used, not the gross deferred tax asset.

q: Gill Co. took a tax position worth a $100,000 tax benefit that is more likely than not to be sustained on examination. The estimated probabilities of the benefit realized on settlement are: $100,000 (30%), $80,000 (25%), $60,000 (25%), and $40,000 (20%). What tax benefit should Gill recognize?
exp: Under ASC 740-10-30-7, the benefit recognized is the largest amount that is more than 50% likely to be realized. Cumulative probabilities are $100,000 at 30% and $80,000 at 55%, so recognize $80,000. Recognizing $100,000 ignores the measurement step that follows recognition.

q: Hart Co. claimed a $50,000 tax benefit for a deduction on its tax return. Management concludes that the position is not more likely than not to be sustained on examination by the taxing authority, based on its technical merits. How should Hart account for the position?
choices: Recognize the $50,000 benefit and disclose the uncertainty
Recognize a benefit equal to the probability-weighted expected value
Recognize no benefit and record a $50,000 liability for the unrecognized tax benefit
Recognize 50% of the benefit
exp: A position that fails the more-likely-than-not recognition threshold gets no benefit; the benefit claimed on the return is recorded as a liability for unrecognized tax benefits (ASC 740-10-25-6). Probability weighting is not used under ASC 740's two-step model.

q: Ivey Co. had a deferred tax liability of $300,000, based on $1,000,000 of taxable temporary differences and a 30% rate. During the year, legislation was enacted lowering the rate to 21% for all future years. How should Ivey account for the change?
choices: Recognize a $90,000 deferred tax benefit in income from continuing operations in the period of enactment
Adjust beginning retained earnings by $90,000
Recognize the effect prospectively as the temporary differences reverse
Recognize a $90,000 gain in other comprehensive income
exp: The effect of an enacted rate change on existing deferred tax balances is recognized in income from continuing operations in the period that includes the enactment date (ASC 740-10-35-4): DTL falls to $210,000, giving a $90,000 benefit. A retained earnings adjustment would treat it like an error correction.

q: Joss Corp. had pretax income from continuing operations of $500,000 and a pretax loss from discontinued operations of $100,000. The tax rate is 25%. Under intraperiod tax allocation, what income tax expense should be reported in income from continuing operations?
exp: Intraperiod allocation assigns tax to continuing operations first, on its own income: $500,000 x 25% = $125,000; the $25,000 benefit is allocated to discontinued operations, which is reported net at $75,000. $100,000 is total tax on combined income.

q: At the end of Year 2, Kemp Co. had $240,000 of cumulative taxable temporary differences on equipment, and its deferred tax liability at the beginning of Year 2 was $45,000. Taxable income for Year 2 was $600,000. The enacted rate is 25% for all years, and there are no other differences. What total income tax expense should Kemp report for Year 2?
exp: Current tax = $600,000 x 25% = $150,000. Ending DTL = $240,000 x 25% = $60,000, so deferred expense = $60,000 - $45,000 = $15,000; total = $165,000. $210,000 adds the entire ending DTL instead of the change in it.

q: Lund Co., a public company, recorded $1,500,000 of goodwill in a taxable business combination; the tax basis of the goodwill is also $1,500,000. For tax purposes the goodwill is amortized over 15 years; for book purposes it is not amortized and is not impaired in Year 1. At a 25% rate, what deferred tax balance related to goodwill should Lund report at the end of Year 1?
choices: Deferred tax asset of $25,000
No deferred tax, because goodwill is excluded from deferred tax accounting
Deferred tax liability of $25,000
Deferred tax liability of $375,000
exp: After Year 1, the book basis ($1,500,000) exceeds the tax basis ($1,400,000) by $100,000, a taxable temporary difference: $100,000 x 25% = $25,000 DTL. The exception that bars recognizing deferred taxes applies only to the excess of book goodwill over tax-deductible goodwill at acquisition.

q: Mead Co.'s pretax income was $200,000 in Q1 and $250,000 in Q2. At the end of Q1, Mead estimated its annual effective tax rate at 24%; at the end of Q2 it revised the estimate to 26%. What income tax expense should Mead report for Q2?
exp: Interim tax = year-to-date income x current estimated annual effective rate, less tax already reported (ASC 740-270): $450,000 x 26% = $117,000, less Q1's $48,000 = $69,000. $65,000 applies the new rate only to Q2 income and omits the catch-up on Q1.

q: Nolan Co. has a deferred tax asset in the U.S. federal jurisdiction and a deferred tax liability in a foreign jurisdiction. How should these be presented on Nolan's balance sheet?
choices: Netted into a single noncurrent amount
Netted into a single current amount
Both omitted, because they offset
Presented separately as a noncurrent asset and a noncurrent liability
exp: Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only within the same tax-paying component and jurisdiction (ASC 740-10-45-6). Balances in different jurisdictions are shown separately, all as noncurrent.

q: In Year 1, Orr Co. sold land with a $300,000 gain, which it recognized in full for financial reporting. For tax purposes the sale qualifies for the installment method, and one-third of the proceeds were collected in Year 1. The enacted tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax liability should Orr report at the end of Year 1?
exp: Two-thirds of the gain ($200,000) will be taxed in future years, creating a taxable temporary difference: $200,000 x 25% = $50,000. $75,000 applies the rate to the whole gain, but one-third has already been taxed.

q: Pyle Co. holds equity securities with readily determinable fair values. During the year it recognized a $40,000 unrealized holding gain in net income; the gain is taxable only when the securities are sold. The tax rate is 25%. How should Pyle report the related deferred tax?
choices: Deferred tax liability of $10,000, with deferred tax expense in net income
Deferred tax liability of $10,000, recorded in other comprehensive income
Deferred tax asset of $10,000
No deferred tax, because the gain is unrealized
exp: Since ASU 2016-01, changes in fair value of equity securities go to net income, so the $40,000 book-over-tax basis difference creates a $10,000 DTL whose tax effect is also in net income. OCI applies to AFS debt securities, not equity securities.

q: Which of the following is the strongest positive evidence supporting the conclusion that no valuation allowance is needed for a deferred tax asset?
choices: Cumulative losses in recent years
A history of operating loss carryforwards expiring unused
Losses expected in early future years by a currently profitable entity
Existing contracts or a sales backlog that will produce enough taxable income to realize the asset
exp: ASC 740-10-30-22 lists existing contracts or a firm sales backlog as positive evidence. The other three items are examples of negative evidence, and cumulative losses in recent years are especially hard to overcome.

q: Quin Co. holds available-for-sale debt securities that increased in fair value by $80,000 during the year. The gain is taxable only when the securities are sold, and the tax rate is 25%. Where should the related $20,000 deferred tax expense be reported?
choices: In income tax expense in income from continuing operations
In other comprehensive income, netted against the unrealized gain
As a direct reduction of retained earnings
It is not recognized until the securities are sold
exp: Under intraperiod tax allocation, the tax effect follows the item that caused it. The unrealized AFS gain is reported in OCI, so its $20,000 deferred tax is also charged to OCI and the gain appears net at $60,000. Charging it to continuing operations would mismatch the tax and the gain.

q: On October 1, Rusk Co. paid a 12-month insurance premium of $48,000, which was deductible in full for tax in the year paid. For book purposes, $36,000 was reported as prepaid insurance at December 31. The tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax amount arises from the prepaid insurance at December 31?
choices: Deferred tax asset of $9,000
Deferred tax liability of $12,000
Deferred tax liability of $9,000
Deferred tax asset of $3,000
exp: The prepaid asset has a $36,000 book basis and a zero tax basis, so future book expense will not be deductible: a taxable temporary difference creating a DTL of $36,000 x 25% = $9,000. A deferred tax asset reverses the direction of the difference.

q: Sora Co. accrued a $200,000 litigation loss that will be deductible for tax purposes when paid, which is expected in two years. The enacted federal rate is 21%, and realization of deferred tax assets is more likely than not. What should Sora record related to the accrual?
choices: A deferred tax liability of $42,000
A deferred tax asset of $42,000
A current tax receivable of $42,000
No deferred tax, because the loss is contingent
exp: The accrued liability has a book basis of $200,000 and a tax basis of zero, producing future deductions: a deductible temporary difference and a deferred tax asset of $200,000 x 21% = $42,000. Nothing is currently refundable, so a receivable is wrong.

q: When employees exercise stock options, Tobin Co. receives a tax deduction that exceeds the cumulative book compensation cost recognized for the awards. Under current GAAP, how should Tobin recognize the excess tax benefit?
choices: As a credit to additional paid-in capital
As a reduction of goodwill
As a deferred tax asset to be realized in future years
As a reduction of income tax expense in the income statement
exp: ASU 2016-09 requires all excess tax benefits and tax deficiencies on share-based payments to be recognized in income tax expense in the period they arise. Crediting APIC (the APIC pool approach) was eliminated.

q: Ulm Corp. received $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10%; the dividends are included in its $1,000,000 of pretax financial income. The dividends qualify for a 50% dividends-received deduction, and there are no other differences. At a 21% federal rate, what is Ulm's current federal income tax expense?
exp: The DRD is a permanent difference: taxable income = $1,000,000 - $50,000 = $950,000, x 21% = $199,500. $195,300 uses the 70% DRD that applied to less-than-20%-owned corporations before the TCJA.

q: On December 15, Year 1, Congress was debating a bill that would lower the corporate rate from 21% to 18% for Year 2 and later. The bill had not been enacted when Vance Co. issued its Year 1 financial statements. What rate should Vance use to measure deferred taxes at December 31, Year 1?
choices: 18%, because it is expected to apply when the differences reverse
A probability-weighted blend of 21% and 18%
21%, the enacted rate
18% for deferred tax liabilities and 21% for deferred tax assets
exp: ASC 740 measures deferred taxes using enacted tax law and rates; expected or proposed changes are not anticipated. The effect of a change is recognized only in the period of enactment.

q: In a nontaxable business combination, the fair value assigned to the acquiree's identifiable assets exceeds their carryover tax basis by $400,000. The enacted rate is 25%. What is the effect on the acquisition accounting?
choices: A $100,000 deferred tax liability is recognized, increasing goodwill by $100,000
No deferred tax is recognized, because the basis differences arose in an acquisition
A $100,000 deferred tax asset is recognized, reducing goodwill
A $100,000 deferred tax liability is recognized in income tax expense
exp: ASC 805-740 requires deferred taxes for differences between assigned values and tax bases of the identifiable assets acquired. The $100,000 DTL reduces net identifiable assets and so increases goodwill; it does not hit income tax expense at acquisition.

q: How may a company classify interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits in its income statement?
choices: Interest must be classified as income tax expense; penalties as operating expense
Both must be classified as income tax expense
As income tax expense or as interest/other expense, based on an accounting policy election applied consistently
Both must be charged directly to retained earnings
exp: ASC 740-10-45-25 allows a policy election to classify interest as income tax expense or interest expense, and penalties as income tax expense or another expense, applied consistently and disclosed. Neither classification is mandatory.

q: Wolfe Co. reported an allowance for uncollectible accounts of $80,000 at year-end. Bad debts are deductible for tax only when written off (direct write-off method), and the enacted tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax amount arises from the allowance?
choices: Deferred tax liability of $20,000
Deferred tax asset of $16,800
No deferred tax, because bad debts are a permanent difference
Deferred tax asset of $20,000
exp: The receivable's tax basis exceeds its book basis by the $80,000 allowance, which will be deducted when written off: a deductible temporary difference and DTA of $80,000 x 25% = $20,000. A DTL would arise only if book basis exceeded tax basis.

q: At the end of Year 1, Xeno Co. had a $120,000 valuation allowance against deferred tax assets from prior operating losses. Because of sustained profitability during Year 2, management now judges that all of the deferred tax assets are more likely than not to be realized in future years. How should Xeno account for eliminating the allowance in Year 2?
choices: As a $120,000 increase in beginning retained earnings
As a $120,000 deferred tax benefit in income from continuing operations
As a $120,000 credit to other comprehensive income
It should be released ratably as the deferred tax assets are realized
exp: A change in judgment about the realizability of beginning-of-year deferred tax assets is a change in estimate, recognized in income from continuing operations in the period of the change (ASC 740-10-45-20). Adjusting retained earnings would treat it like an error correction.
